Similarly, in software testing, test doubles step in to replace real components, making testing simpler, faster, and more reliable.

entry.title: iOS Accessibility Basics
entry.content:
iOS accessibility is about building apps that people with disabilities can use as fully and independently as everyone else. Apple ships a remarkable set of assistive technologies with every iPhone and iPad, from the VoiceOver screen reader to Voice Control and Switch Control, and it gives developers the APIs to make their apps work with all of them. Apple’s accessibility site is the official starting point.

The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.3 billion people, roughly 1 in 6 of us, live with a significant disability. Add the people who are temporarily injured, getting older, or just using their phone one-handed on a bright, noisy street, and accessibility stops being an edge case. It’s simply part of building a good app.

The good news: most of the work is small, concrete, and much cheaper when you do it from the start. This post covers why accessibility matters, then walks through the practical side: what each assistive technology needs from your app, the SwiftUI and UIKit APIs that provide it, and how to test the result.

Building accessible and inclusive iOS interfaces

Why Accessibility Matters

Making your app accessible opens it to people with visual, hearing, motor, speech, and cognitive disabilities, many of whom rely on their iPhone more than anyone: to read mail, recognize objects, navigate cities, and talk to the people they love. If your app doesn’t work with VoiceOver, for a blind user it simply doesn’t work.

Accessibility also tends to improve the app for everyone. This is known as the curb-cut effect, after the sidewalk ramps designed for wheelchair users that turned out to help everyone pushing a stroller or pulling a suitcase. Captions help people in loud places, larger text helps tired eyes, clear labels help people new to your app, and good contrast helps everyone outdoors.

Why Accessibility Gets Overlooked

Many teams skip accessibility for reasons that don’t hold up:

  1. Lack of awareness. Many developers have never seen someone use VoiceOver, so they don’t know what’s broken.
  2. Perceived complexity. It looks like a big, specialized field. In practice, standard UIKit and SwiftUI controls are accessible out of the box, and most of the remaining work is a handful of modifiers.
  3. Misaligned priorities. Visual polish and new features win, and accessibility is pushed to “later”, which is when it becomes expensive.
  4. Cost. Retrofitting an app is costly. Building it accessibly from the start usually isn’t.
  5. “Our users don’t need it.” Disabilities are common, often invisible, and many people don’t call themselves “disabled” even though they use larger text or captions every day.

Laws and Standards

This section is a general overview, not legal advice. Requirements depend on where you operate and who your users are.

Standards: WCAG

The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are the most widely used accessibility standard. They’re published by the W3C through its Web Accessibility Initiative (WAI). The current version is WCAG 2.2 (2023), and most laws reference level AA of WCAG 2.1 or 2.2. WCAG was written for the web, but the W3C’s WCAG2ICT guidance explains how to apply it to native apps, and most of it carries over directly: text alternatives, contrast ratios, resizable text, no information conveyed by color alone, and so on.

Meeting WCAG doesn’t automatically make an app pleasant to use with assistive technology, and it doesn’t by itself guarantee legal compliance. It’s still the best yardstick available.

Laws in the United States

  • The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) prohibits discrimination by businesses open to the public (Title III) and by state and local governments (Title II). The ADA doesn’t mention apps or websites explicitly, and courts have disagreed about how far Title III reaches, but thousands of digital accessibility lawsuits are filed every year.
  • In 2024, the Department of Justice issued a rule under Title II that requires state and local governments’ websites and mobile apps to meet WCAG 2.1 level AA, with compliance dates in 2026 and 2027 depending on the size of the government.
  • Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act requires federal agencies to make the technology they build, buy, and use accessible. (Organizations that receive federal funding are covered by a different part of the same law, Section 504.)

Laws in Europe and elsewhere

  • The European Accessibility Act (EAA) has applied since June 28, 2025. It covers many consumer products and services sold in the EU, including e-commerce, banking, e-books, and passenger transport services, and their apps. Its technical requirements are based on the European standard EN 301 549, which in turn includes WCAG.
  • Many other countries have their own laws, such as Canada’s Accessible Canada Act and Ontario’s AODA, often also built on WCAG.

What has happened in court

A few cases are often cited:

  • National Federation of the Blind v. Target (2006–2008): A federal court allowed claims that Target’s inaccessible website violated the ADA, because of its connection to Target’s physical stores. The case settled for $6 million.
  • National Association of the Deaf v. Netflix (2012): A court held that the ADA could apply to a web-only streaming service. Netflix settled and agreed to caption all of its content.
  • Robles v. Domino’s Pizza (2019): The Ninth Circuit ruled that the ADA applied to Domino’s website and app, because they connected customers to its physical restaurants. The Supreme Court declined to hear Domino’s appeal, and the case settled in 2022.

None of these ended with a final judgment that set the rules for every app. They’re important because they show that courts take digital accessibility seriously, and most businesses choose to settle and fix their apps rather than fight.

The consequences of ignoring it

  • Lawsuits and settlements: Legal fees, settlements, and court-ordered remediation plans.
  • Fines: Under laws like the EAA, regulators can impose penalties.
  • Reputation: People notice, and people with disabilities and their families talk to each other.
  • Lost users: The most common consequence, and the quietest one. People who can’t use your app just leave.

How People Use Their iPhones: Apple’s Assistive Technologies

Before writing any code, it helps to know what you’re building for. Here are the main assistive technologies built into iOS and iPadOS, all found under Settings → Accessibility:

Technology Who it helps What it needs from your app
VoiceOver Blind and low-vision users Every element has a meaningful label, the right traits, and a sensible reading order.
Dynamic Type / Larger Text Low-vision users, older users, anyone Text that scales, and layouts that adapt instead of truncating.
Voice Control People who can’t use touch Visible text and labels that match what users would naturally say.
Switch Control People with limited mobility who use one or more switches Elements reachable in a logical order, with actions available without complex gestures.
AssistiveTouch People who find gestures or physical buttons difficult Alternatives to gestures like pinch, shake, or long press.
Full Keyboard Access Keyboard users, especially on iPad Every control reachable and usable with a keyboard.
Display settings (Increase Contrast, Reduce Transparency, Bold Text, Button Shapes, Smart Invert, Differentiate Without Color) Low-vision and color-blind users Respect these settings instead of overriding them.
Reduce Motion People with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity Gentler alternatives to large animations, parallax, and auto-playing motion.
Captions, Audio Descriptions, Live Captions Deaf, hard-of-hearing, and blind users Caption tracks and audio descriptions for media, no information conveyed by sound alone.
Assistive Access, Guided Access People with cognitive disabilities Simple, predictable flows.
Live Speech, Personal Voice People who can’t speak, or are losing their voice Don’t require voice input for core features.

The rest of this post goes through these one by one, with code. Most of the APIs exist in both SwiftUI and UIKit; I’ll show SwiftUI first and UIKit where it differs.

VoiceOver: Labels, Values, Traits, and Hints

VoiceOver reads the element under the user’s finger, and users swipe left and right to move between elements. For each element, it typically reads four pieces of information:

Property Example Question it answers
Label “Volume” What is this?
Value “60 percent” What is its current state?
Traits “adjustable”, “button”, “selected”, “heading” What kind of thing is it, and how does it behave?
Hint “Swipe up or down to adjust.” What happens if I use it? (optional, read after a pause)

Standard controls like Button, Toggle, Slider, and UISwitch fill most of this in automatically. Your job is mostly to fix what the system can’t guess.

Label icon-only buttons

This is the single most common VoiceOver bug. A button with only an image has no text for VoiceOver to read:

Button {
    toggleFavorite()
} label: {
    Image(systemName: isFavorite ? "heart.fill" : "heart")
}
.accessibilityLabel("Favorite")
.accessibilityAddTraits(isFavorite ? .isSelected : [])

VoiceOver now reads “Favorite, selected, button” instead of a guess based on the symbol’s name (or worse, the image’s file name). In UIKit:

favoriteButton.accessibilityLabel = "Favorite"
favoriteButton.accessibilityTraits = isFavorite ? [.button, .selected] : .button

An even better option in SwiftUI is to use a Label, which gives you a text label for free and lets the style decide what’s visible:

Button(action: toggleFavorite) {
    Label("Favorite", systemImage: "heart")
}
.labelStyle(.iconOnly) // shows only the icon, VoiceOver still reads "Favorite"

Write good labels

Apple’s guidelines for labels:

  • Be short and specific: “Add to cart”, not “This button adds the current item to your shopping cart”.
  • Don’t include the control type. VoiceOver already says “button”, so “Play button” is read as “Play button, button”.
  • Start with a capital letter and don’t end with a period. VoiceOver reads labels better that way.
  • Describe what it is, not what it looks like: “Delete”, not “Trash can”.
  • Localize them. Labels are user-facing text like any other. accessibilityLabel in SwiftUI accepts localized string keys, so add them to your string catalog.

Hints are optional and are read after a short pause, if the user hasn’t turned them off. Use them only when the result of an action isn’t obvious, and describe the result rather than the gesture: “Plays the song”, not “Double-tap to play the song”. VoiceOver users already know how to activate things.

Hide decorative images, describe meaningful ones

Images that are purely decorative should be skipped entirely, so users don’t swipe through noise:

Image(decorative: "background-wave")       // never read by VoiceOver

Image("divider")
    .accessibilityHidden(true)              // same, for any view

Meaningful images need a label that describes what matters about them in context:

Image("chart-weekly-sales")
    .accessibilityLabel("Weekly sales, up 12 percent from last week")

In UIKit, images aren’t accessibility elements by default. Set isAccessibilityElement = true and an accessibilityLabel for meaningful ones.

Group related content

Without grouping, a list row with a name, a price, a rating, and a thumbnail can take four or five swipes. Combine it into one element:

HStack {
    Image(product.imageName)
        .accessibilityHidden(true)
    VStack(alignment: .leading) {
        Text(product.name)
        Text(product.price, format: .currency(code: "USD"))
    }
    Spacer()
    RatingView(rating: product.rating)
}
.accessibilityElement(children: .combine)

.combine joins the children’s labels, so VoiceOver reads the whole row in one go. If the automatic result reads awkwardly, use .ignore and write the label yourself:

.accessibilityElement(children: .ignore)
.accessibilityLabel("\(product.name), \(product.formattedPrice), rated \(product.rating) out of 5")

In UIKit, make the cell itself the accessibility element: set isAccessibilityElement = true on the cell and give it an accessibilityLabel built from its contents.

Use the right traits

Traits tell VoiceOver what an element is:

  • .isButton for anything tappable that isn’t a real Button. In SwiftUI, a view with .onTapGesture is not a button to VoiceOver, so prefer a real Button with a custom style.
  • .isHeader for section titles. VoiceOver users can jump between headings with the rotor (a two-finger twisting gesture), which makes long screens much faster to navigate.
  • .isSelected for the current tab, the chosen option, a toggled-on state.
  • .isLink, .isImage, .isSearchField, .updatesFrequently, and others for their matching roles.
Text("Recent Orders")
    .font(.headline)
    .accessibilityAddTraits(.isHeader)

Expose values and adjustable controls

A custom control needs to tell VoiceOver its state and let users change it. Take a five-star rating view:

struct RatingView: View {
    @Binding var rating: Int

    var body: some View {
        HStack {
            ForEach(1...5, id: \.self) { star in
                Image(systemName: star <= rating ? "star.fill" : "star")
                    .onTapGesture { rating = star }
            }
        }
        .accessibilityElement()
        .accessibilityLabel("Rating")
        .accessibilityValue("\(rating) out of 5 stars")
        .accessibilityAdjustableAction { direction in
            switch direction {
            case .increment: rating = min(rating + 1, 5)
            case .decrement: rating = max(rating - 1, 1)
            @unknown default: break
            }
        }
    }
}

VoiceOver reads “Rating, 3 out of 5 stars, adjustable”, and the user swipes up or down to change it, instead of hunting for five separate tiny stars. In UIKit, add the .adjustable trait and override accessibilityIncrement() and accessibilityDecrement().

If a custom control behaves exactly like a standard one, SwiftUI’s .accessibilityRepresentation lets you hand VoiceOver a standard control to describe it:

CustomToggleView(isOn: $isOn)
    .accessibilityRepresentation {
        Toggle("Notifications", isOn: $isOn)
    }

Replace gestures with custom actions

Swipe-to-delete, long-press menus, and drag-and-drop are hard or impossible for many assistive technology users. Custom actions put them in a list VoiceOver users reach by swiping up or down, and Switch Control and Voice Control can use them too:

MessageRow(message: message)
    .accessibilityAction(named: "Reply") { reply(to: message) }
    .accessibilityAction(named: "Archive") { archive(message) }
    .accessibilityAction(named: "Delete") { delete(message) }

In UIKit:

cell.accessibilityCustomActions = [
    UIAccessibilityCustomAction(name: "Reply") { _ in self.reply(to: message); return true },
    UIAccessibilityCustomAction(name: "Delete") { _ in self.delete(message); return true }
]

This also keeps rows to a single swipe stop, instead of exposing every small button inside them.

Control reading order and focus

VoiceOver reads elements roughly from top-left to bottom-right (or top-right to bottom-left in right-to-left languages). When your layout doesn’t match the logical order, for example a big number shown above its title, adjust it:

VStack {
    Text("72°")
        .accessibilitySortPriority(1) // read second
    Text("Current temperature")
        .accessibilitySortPriority(2) // read first: higher priority goes first
}
.accessibilityElement(children: .contain)

When something important appears or changes, move VoiceOver’s focus to it or announce it. @AccessibilityFocusState moves focus in SwiftUI:

struct LoginForm: View {
    @State private var errorMessage: String?
    @AccessibilityFocusState private var isErrorFocused: Bool

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            if let errorMessage {
                Text(errorMessage)
                    .foregroundStyle(.red)
                    .accessibilityFocused($isErrorFocused)
            }
            Button("Sign In", action: signIn)
        }
    }

    private func signIn() {
        errorMessage = "Incorrect password. Try again."
        isErrorFocused = true
    }
}

For short-lived status messages that shouldn’t steal focus, post an announcement:

AccessibilityNotification.Announcement("Saved to Favorites").post() // iOS 17+

In UIKit, use UIAccessibility.post(notification: .announcement, argument: "Saved to Favorites"). When a large part of the screen changes, post .screenChanged (for a new screen) or .layoutChanged (for a smaller change), optionally passing the element to focus as the argument.

Two more UIKit details are easy to miss when building custom popups and overlays:

  • Set accessibilityViewIsModal = true on the overlay, so VoiceOver doesn’t wander into the content behind it. SwiftUI’s sheets, alerts, and popovers do this for you.
  • Override accessibilityPerformEscape() to dismiss it, so the VoiceOver “escape” gesture (a two-finger Z-shaped scrub) works. In SwiftUI, use .accessibilityAction(.escape) { dismiss() } on custom overlays.

Dynamic Type: Text That Scales

Dynamic Type lets people choose their preferred text size in Settings → Accessibility → Display & Text Size → Larger Text. There are seven standard sizes, plus five much larger accessibility sizes (AX1 to AX5) once the user turns on Larger Accessibility Sizes. At the largest size, body text is more than three times the default.

A large share of iPhone users change their text size from the default, so this is one of the most-used accessibility features of all.

Use text styles

In SwiftUI, the built-in text styles scale automatically:

Text("Order summary")
    .font(.headline)

Text(order.details)
    .font(.body)

For custom fonts, tell SwiftUI which text style to scale with:

Text("Welcome back")
    .font(.custom("Avenir Next", size: 28, relativeTo: .title))

.font(.system(size: 17)) and .font(.custom("Avenir Next", fixedSize: 17)) do not scale. Avoid them for anything people need to read.

Use @ScaledMetric for non-text sizes that should grow with the text, like icons and spacing:

@ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .body) private var iconSize: CGFloat = 24

Image(systemName: "bell")
    .frame(width: iconSize, height: iconSize)

In UIKit, use preferred fonts and turn on automatic updates. UIFontMetrics handles custom fonts:

// System font
titleLabel.font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle: .headline)
titleLabel.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true
titleLabel.numberOfLines = 0

// Custom font
let avenir = UIFont(name: "AvenirNext-Regular", size: 17)!
bodyLabel.font = UIFontMetrics(forTextStyle: .body).scaledFont(for: avenir)
bodyLabel.adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true
bodyLabel.numberOfLines = 0

Without adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory, the font is only correct for the text size at the moment you set it, and doesn’t update when the user changes the setting while the app is running.

Make layouts adapt

Scaling text is the easy part. The real work is making sure the layout survives it:

  • Let text wrap. Avoid lineLimit(1) and numberOfLines = 1 for meaningful content, and avoid fixed heights on text containers.
  • Put scrollable content in a ScrollView or table/collection view, so it can grow beyond the screen.
  • Switch from horizontal to vertical layouts at large sizes. Side-by-side content that fits at the default size will be crushed at AX5:
struct ContactRow: View {
    @Environment(\.dynamicTypeSize) private var dynamicTypeSize
    let contact: Contact

    var body: some View {
        let layout = dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize
            ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(alignment: .leading))
            : AnyLayout(HStackLayout())

        layout {
            Text(contact.name).font(.headline)
            Spacer()
            Text(contact.phone).font(.body)
        }
    }
}

AnyLayout keeps the children’s identity when the layout changes, so state and animations are preserved. Another option is ViewThatFits, which picks the first layout that fits the available space.

In UIKit, check traitCollection.preferredContentSizeCategory.isAccessibilityCategory and switch a UIStackView’s axis from .horizontal to .vertical.

Large Content Viewer for UI that can’t grow

Some elements, like tab bars, toolbars, and segmented controls, can’t grow much without breaking the layout. For those, iOS offers the Large Content Viewer: when the user long-presses the element at an accessibility text size, a large version of its icon and title appears in the middle of the screen. System tab bars and toolbars support it automatically. For custom ones:

CustomTabButton(title: "Library", systemImage: "books.vertical")
    .accessibilityShowsLargeContentViewer {
        Label("Library", systemImage: "books.vertical")
    }

In UIKit, set showsLargeContentViewer = true on the view and add a UILargeContentViewerInteraction to its container.

Color, Contrast, and Display Settings

Meet contrast ratios

WCAG level AA requires a contrast ratio of at least:

  • 4.5:1 for regular text,
  • 3:1 for large text (roughly 18 points, or 14 points bold, and larger),
  • 3:1 for icons, borders of input fields, and other graphics people need in order to understand or use the interface.

Light gray text on a white background is the classic failure. The Accessibility Inspector in Xcode includes a color contrast calculator, and the automated audit described below flags low contrast too.

Don’t rely on color alone

About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some form of color vision deficiency, most commonly red-green. Never make color the only way to convey something: pair it with an icon, text, or a pattern. A form field with an error should show a message and an icon, not just a red border. A chart’s lines should differ in shape or be labeled directly.

Users can also ask apps to do this explicitly with Differentiate Without Color:

@Environment(\.accessibilityDifferentiateWithoutColor) private var differentiateWithoutColor

var statusIndicator: some View {
    HStack {
        Circle()
            .fill(isOnline ? .green : .red)
            .frame(width: 10, height: 10)
        if differentiateWithoutColor {
            Image(systemName: isOnline ? "checkmark" : "xmark")
        }
    }
}

Respect the user’s display settings

System colors (.primary, .secondary, Color(.systemBackground), UIColor.label, and so on) automatically adapt to Dark Mode and to Increase Contrast. For your own colors, add a High Contrast variant in the asset catalog (select the color set, then check High Contrast under Appearances in the Attributes inspector), and the system picks it automatically.

Some settings to check for when you draw custom UI:

Setting SwiftUI UIKit
Increase Contrast @Environment(\.colorSchemeContrast) traitCollection.accessibilityContrast
Reduce Transparency @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceTransparency) UIAccessibility.isReduceTransparencyEnabled
Bold Text @Environment(\.legibilityWeight) UIAccessibility.isBoldTextEnabled
Button Shapes @Environment(\.accessibilityShowButtonShapes) UIAccessibility.buttonShapesEnabled
Smart Invert .accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors() accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors

Smart Invert inverts the colors of the interface but tries to leave photos and videos alone. Mark your images, video players, and maps with .accessibilityIgnoresInvertColors() so they don’t appear as negatives.

Motion and Animation

Large animations, parallax, and zooming transitions can cause dizziness and nausea for people with vestibular disorders. When Reduce Motion is on, replace them with gentler effects, like a cross-fade, rather than removing feedback entirely:

@Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion) private var reduceMotion

var body: some View {
    DetailCard()
        .transition(reduceMotion ? .opacity : .move(edge: .bottom))
}

In UIKit, check UIAccessibility.isReduceMotionEnabled and observe UIAccessibility.reduceMotionStatusDidChangeNotification.

Also:

  • Don’t auto-play video when UIAccessibility.isVideoAutoplayEnabled is false.
  • Give users a way to pause, stop, or hide anything that moves for more than five seconds (WCAG 2.2.2).
  • Never flash anything more than three times per second (WCAG 2.3.1). Flashing content can trigger seizures.

Motor Accessibility: Touch Targets, Voice Control, and Switches

Make targets big enough

Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines recommend touch targets of at least 44×44 points. The visible icon can be smaller; the tappable area shouldn’t be:

Button(action: close) {
    Image(systemName: "xmark")
        .frame(minWidth: 44, minHeight: 44)
        .contentShape(Rectangle()) // the whole frame is tappable, not just the glyph
}
.accessibilityLabel("Close")

Leave space between targets too, so a slightly-off tap doesn’t hit the wrong control.

Provide alternatives to complex gestures

Pinching, multi-finger swipes, shaking, precise dragging, and long presses are hard for many people. Every action reachable through such a gesture should also be available through a simple tap: a visible button, a menu, or at least a custom accessibility action as shown above.

Avoid time limits where you can. If a session must expire, warn the user and let them extend it.

Support Voice Control

Voice Control lets people use their device entirely by speaking: “Tap Send”, “Scroll down”, “Show numbers”. It uses your accessibility labels as the names people speak, which is one more reason they should be short and match the visible text. A button that shows “Send” but has the label “Submit message” can’t be activated by saying what the user sees.

When people might naturally use several names for one control, give Voice Control alternatives:

Button("Compose", action: compose)
    .accessibilityInputLabels(["Compose", "New message", "Write"])

In UIKit, set accessibilityUserInputLabels.

Switch Control and Full Keyboard Access

Switch Control users move through the screen one element at a time with a switch or two, and Full Keyboard Access users do the same with Tab and the arrow keys. Both depend on the same foundation as VoiceOver: a logical element order, sensible grouping (one stop per list row, not five), and actions that don’t require gestures. If your app works well with VoiceOver, it usually works well with these too. Still, test them, because custom controls that ignore focus are a common failure.

Hearing Accessibility

  • Caption your videos. AVPlayerViewController (and SwiftUI’s VideoPlayer) shows closed captions and subtitles automatically when the media includes caption tracks and the user has enabled them in Settings → Accessibility → Subtitles & Captioning. Your job is to provide the tracks. If you build a custom player, respect the setting with MACaptionAppearanceGetDisplayType from the MediaAccessibility framework.
  • Add audio descriptions when important information in a video is only shown visually. This helps blind users.
  • Never convey information through sound alone. Pair alert sounds with something visible, and consider haptics:
Button("Pay", action: pay)
    .sensoryFeedback(.success, trigger: paymentSucceeded) // iOS 17+
  • Offer transcripts for podcasts and audio-only content.

Cognitive Accessibility

Cognitive disabilities affect memory, attention, reading, and problem solving, and they’re the most common kind of disability. They are also the hardest to address with a single API, because most of the work is good design:

  • Use plain language. Short sentences, familiar words, no jargon.
  • Be consistent. Keep navigation and controls in the same place across screens, and call the same thing by the same name everywhere.
  • Write useful error messages. Say what went wrong and how to fix it: “Password must be at least 8 characters”, not “Invalid input”.
  • Let people undo. Confirm destructive actions, and offer undo where you can.
  • Reduce distractions. Limit auto-playing content, pop-ups, and timers.
  • Don’t rely on memory. Show the information people need on the screen where they need it, instead of expecting them to remember it from a previous step.

iOS also offers Guided Access, which locks the device to one app, and Assistive Access, a simplified version of iOS with large buttons and a reduced set of apps. Clear, simple flows in your own app make both work better.

Speech Accessibility

People with speech disabilities may not be able to use voice input, or may use an AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) app to speak for them. iOS also includes Live Speech, which speaks typed text aloud, and Personal Voice, which lets people at risk of losing their voice create a synthesized version of it.

For your app, the rule is simple: never make voice the only way in. Anything that can be done by speaking, like voice search or a voice assistant, should also be possible by typing or tapping.

Types of Disabilities: A Summary

Disability type What to do
Visual (blindness, low vision, color blindness) Label every element for VoiceOver, support Dynamic Type at all sizes, meet contrast ratios, never rely on color alone, and respect Increase Contrast, Bold Text, and Smart Invert.
Hearing Caption videos, provide transcripts, pair sounds with visual cues and haptics.
Motor Make targets at least 44×44 points, offer alternatives to complex gestures and time limits, and support Voice Control, Switch Control, and Full Keyboard Access.
Vestibular Respect Reduce Motion, avoid parallax and large zooming transitions, never flash content.
Cognitive Use plain language, consistent navigation, clear error messages, undo, and fewer distractions.
Speech Never require voice input; always offer a typed or tapped alternative.
Situational and temporary (bright sun, noisy room, a broken arm, holding a baby) The same features help everyone: captions, good contrast, larger text, one-handed reachability.

Testing Accessibility

You can’t know whether your app is accessible without using it the way your users do. A good routine mixes manual testing, tools, and automation.

Test with VoiceOver on a real device

  1. Set up the Accessibility Shortcut under Settings → Accessibility → Accessibility Shortcut and choose VoiceOver. Now triple-clicking the side button (or Home button) turns VoiceOver on and off.
  2. Learn the basic gestures: tap to select and hear an element, swipe right/left to move to the next/previous element, double-tap to activate, two-finger swipe up to read the whole screen, and three-finger swipe to scroll.
  3. Go through your app’s main flows using only those gestures. For the real experience, turn on Screen Curtain (a three-finger triple-tap with VoiceOver on), which turns the display off so you can’t cheat by looking.

Ask yourself: Can I reach everything? Does every element make sense out of context? Do I know when something changes? Can I complete the task?

Use Xcode’s tools

  • Accessibility Inspector (Xcode → Open Developer Tool → Accessibility Inspector) shows the label, value, traits, and other properties of any element in the simulator or on a connected device. Its Audit tab scans the current screen for common problems, and its color contrast calculator checks color pairs.
  • Environment Overrides, in the debug bar while your app runs, let you switch text size, Increase Contrast, Reduce Motion, Bold Text, and other settings instantly, without leaving Xcode.
  • Xcode Previews can show the same view at every Dynamic Type size at once, using the variants button in the preview canvas.

Automate audits in UI tests

Since Xcode 15 (on iOS 17 and later), UI tests can run the same audit as the Accessibility Inspector:

import XCTest

final class AccessibilityAuditTests: XCTestCase {
    func testHomeScreenPassesAccessibilityAudit() throws {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launch()

        try app.performAccessibilityAudit()
    }

    func testSettingsPassesContrastAndDynamicTypeAudit() throws {
        let app = XCUIApplication()
        app.launch()
        app.buttons["Settings"].tap()

        try app.performAccessibilityAudit(for: [.contrast, .dynamicType]) { issue in
            // Return true to ignore a known issue, false to fail the test.
            issue.element?.identifier == "decorative-banner"
        }
    }
}

The audit checks things like missing labels, low contrast, clipped text at large sizes, small hit regions, and elements that VoiceOver can’t reach. Run it on every important screen in CI, so regressions are caught before they ship. It can’t tell you whether a label is meaningful, though, or whether a flow makes sense, so it complements manual testing rather than replacing it.

Test with real people

The best feedback comes from people who use assistive technology every day. If you can, include users with disabilities in your usability testing, or work with accessibility testing services that employ them.

Show Your Work: Accessibility Nutrition Labels

Since 2025, the App Store lets developers declare which accessibility features their apps support, in Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the product page. You fill them in in App Store Connect for features like VoiceOver, Voice Control, Larger Text, Dark Interface, Differentiate Without Color Alone, Sufficient Contrast, Reduced Motion, Captions, and Audio Descriptions.

Only declare a feature if users can complete your app’s common tasks with it. That’s the bar Apple sets, and it’s a useful checklist in its own right. The labels also give people with disabilities a way to find apps that will actually work for them, which makes accessibility a visible part of your product, not just a hidden quality.

Accessibility Best Practices: A Checklist

Before shipping a screen, check that:

  • Every interactive element has a short, meaningful, localized label, and icon-only buttons are labeled.
  • Decorative images are hidden from VoiceOver; meaningful ones are described.
  • Related content is grouped, so list rows are one swipe stop.
  • Headings have the .isHeader trait.
  • Custom controls expose their value, traits, and actions (adjustable, toggle, selected).
  • Swipe, long-press, and drag actions are also available as buttons or custom actions.
  • Focus moves to, or an announcement is posted for, important changes and errors.
  • All text uses Dynamic Type and the layout works at AX5 without clipping or overlap.
  • Text meets 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text and important graphics) in both light and dark mode.
  • Nothing is conveyed by color, sound, or motion alone.
  • Reduce Motion is respected, and nothing flashes.
  • Touch targets are at least 44×44 points.
  • Videos have captions.
  • The screen passes performAccessibilityAudit() and a manual VoiceOver run-through.

Conclusion

Accessibility isn’t a separate feature you bolt on at the end. It’s a quality of how your app is built, like performance or security, and like those, it’s far cheaper to get right from the start. Standard controls give you a head start, a few modifiers cover most of what remains, and Xcode’s tools make it easy to check your work.

Start small: turn on VoiceOver and try your app’s most important flow with your eyes closed. Then do the same at the largest text size. What you find will be your first to-do list, and fixing it will make your app better for everyone who uses it.

Further Reading

  • Apple Accessibility for developers
  • Human Interface Guidelines: Accessibility
  • WCAG 2.2 and the WCAG2ICT guidance for applying it to apps
  • WWDC sessions: search the Developer app or website for “accessibility”. Every year has several practical sessions, including ones on SwiftUI accessibility and automated audits.
entry.summary: iOS accessibility is about building apps that people with disabilities can use as fully and independently as everyone else. Apple ships a remarkable set of assistive technologies with every iPhone and iPad, from the VoiceOver screen reader to Voice Control and Switch Control, and it gives developers the APIs to make their apps work with all of them. Apple’s accessibility site is the official starting point.

entry.title: SwiftUI Views Are Values, Not Objects: Understanding the Implications

link.title: SwiftUI Views Are Values, Not Objects: Understanding the Implications

entry.content:
In SwiftUI, a view is not a long-lived object sitting on screen. It is a lightweight value, usually a struct, that describes a piece of UI. SwiftUI creates these values, reads them, and throws them away constantly.

That one fact explains a lot of SwiftUI behavior that looks strange if you come from UIKit: why you can’t just assign to a property inside body, why @State sometimes “ignores” a new value you pass in, why a .task keeps working with stale data, and why state can suddenly reset. Let’s look at what “views are values” really means, how SwiftUI uses it to update the screen, and the bugs you get when you forget it. 🧐

SwiftUI views as value snapshots driven by state

A View Is a Description, Not the Thing on Screen

In UIKit, a UILabel is an object. You create it once, keep a reference to it, and change its text over time. The object is the thing on screen.

In SwiftUI, this:

struct Greeting: View {
    let name: String

    var body: some View {
        Text("Hello, \(name)")
            .font(.title)
    }
}

is just a recipe. A Greeting value holds a string and knows how to produce a body. It isn’t rendered, and it has no frame and no lifetime of its own. SwiftUI reads the description and keeps its own, separate, long-lived representation of the UI (internally a dependency graph, often called the attribute graph). That internal representation is what owns the state, the layout results, and the platform views or layers that end up on screen.

So there are two different lifetimes to keep apart:

  • The lifetime of a view value. Very short. A Greeting struct may be created every time its parent’s body runs, then discarded.
  • The lifetime of a view’s identity. As long as SwiftUI considers “this view” to be the same view in the hierarchy. This is where @State storage lives, and it is the span between onAppear and onDisappear (roughly; containers like List can fire these more than once as rows scroll in and out).

Most of the bugs below come from mixing up these two lifetimes.

Why structs?

Making views value types is a deliberate design choice, not just a matter of taste:

  • They’re cheap. A small struct is stored inline and is often just a few bytes. Creating thousands of them per second costs almost nothing, while creating and tearing down class instances means heap allocation and reference counting.
  • No shared mutable state between copies. A view value can’t be changed behind your back by someone holding another reference to it, so the description SwiftUI reads is exactly the one body produced.
  • No inheritance. There’s no UIView-style base class carrying dozens of stored properties. Behavior is added by composition (wrapping views in other views and modifiers) instead.
  • They’re easy to compare. SwiftUI can compare a new view value with the previous one to decide whether anything below it needs updating. More on that below.

What Value Semantics Does (and Doesn’t) Give You

Views aren’t “immutable”, but body can’t mutate them

A view struct can declare var properties, and its initializer can set them however it likes. What you can’t do is mutate self from inside body, because body is a non-mutating computed property:

struct Counter: View {
    var count = 0

    var body: some View {
        Button("Tapped \(count) times") {
            count += 1 // ❌ Cannot assign to property: 'self' is immutable
        }
    }
}

Even if this compiled, it would be pointless: the struct is a throwaway copy, and SwiftUI would make a fresh Counter with count = 0 the next time the parent’s body runs. State that must survive belongs in storage SwiftUI manages for you:

struct Counter: View {
    @State private var count = 0

    var body: some View {
        Button("Tapped \(count) times") {
            count += 1 // ✅ writes to storage owned by SwiftUI, not to the struct
        }
    }
}

@State is a property wrapper. The struct holds a small handle, and the real value lives in SwiftUI’s graph, tied to the view’s identity. That is why it survives the struct being recreated.

Modifiers wrap, they don’t mutate

.font(.title) doesn’t change the Text. It returns a new value of a different type that wraps the original. You can see this by printing the type:

let view = Text("Hi")
    .padding()
    .background(.red)

print(type(of: view))
// ModifiedContent<ModifiedContent<Text, _PaddingLayout>, _BackgroundStyleModifier<Color>>

(The exact internal type names vary between SDK versions, but the nesting is the point.)

Chaining modifiers builds a nested type that describes the whole thing, from the inside out. That’s also why modifier order matters: .padding().background(.red) paints the padding red, while .background(.red).padding() paints only behind the text and adds clear space around it. They are different descriptions, so they produce different results.

Thread safety is not automatic

A common claim is that value types are “inherently thread-safe”. That’s only partially true. Copying a struct gives you an independent copy of its stored values, but if those values include references (an ObservableObject, a class-based model, a closure capturing shared state), the copies still point to the same shared object. Swift models this with Sendable, not with “it’s a struct”.

For SwiftUI specifically, the View protocol is isolated to the main actor (made explicit in the iOS 18 SDK), so body and view initializers run on the main thread anyway. Being a value type is not what keeps your views safe from data races. Main-actor isolation does that.

Who Owns the Data?

Because the view struct itself can’t hold anything durable, every piece of data in a view is either a plain input that gets replaced on each re-creation, or a handle to storage that lives somewhere else. Choosing the right property wrapper is mostly a question of who owns the data and how long it lives:

Declaration Who owns the data Lives as long as
let / var (no wrapper) The parent, passed in One view value (replaced on every re-creation)
@State This view (SwiftUI stores it) This view’s identity
@Binding Someone else; this view can read and write it The owner’s storage
@StateObject This view (for ObservableObject) This view’s identity
@ObservedObject Someone else (for ObservableObject) Whoever owns the object
@State with an @Observable class This view (iOS 17+) This view’s identity
@Environment / @EnvironmentObject An ancestor view The ancestor’s storage

A plain stored property isn’t wrong. It is the right choice for input data the view only displays. It just can’t be the source of truth for anything the view changes.

How SwiftUI Decides What to Update

When state changes, SwiftUI doesn’t rebuild the whole screen, and it doesn’t run a React-style “diff two whole trees” pass either. Roughly:

  1. A piece of state changes, such as a @State value or a property of an @Observable model.
  2. SwiftUI’s dependency graph knows which views read that state while their body ran, so only those views are invalidated.
  3. SwiftUI re-runs body for the invalidated views, producing new child view values.
  4. For each child, it compares the new value with the previous one. If they’re equal, it can skip running that child’s body. If not, the child is updated as well.
  5. Layout and rendering are updated for whatever actually changed.

This works because views are cheap values: creating and comparing them costs far less than creating and tearing down objects. It is also why view initializers and body should be cheap and free of side effects. SwiftUI may call them often, and you don’t control when.

How views are compared

By default SwiftUI compares a view’s stored properties field by field. Simple values like numbers, strings, and Equatable structs compare well. Some things can’t be compared in a meaningful way, closures being the classic example, so a view that stores a closure is often treated as “changed” every time its parent re-renders.

If you know better than SwiftUI which properties matter, you can make the view Equatable and apply .equatable() so SwiftUI uses your ==:

struct ScoreRow: View, Equatable {
    let player: Player
    let onTap: () -> Void

    static func == (lhs: Self, rhs: Self) -> Bool {
        lhs.player.id == rhs.player.id && lhs.player.score == rhs.player.score
    }

    var body: some View {
        Button(player.name, action: onTap)
    }
}

// In the parent:
ScoreRow(player: player, onTap: { select(player) })
    .equatable()

Use this sparingly and only after measuring. If your == ignores something the body actually depends on, the view will show stale content, which is exactly the kind of bug this post is about.

Smaller views mean smaller updates

Each separate View struct gets its own node in SwiftUI’s graph, so it can be compared and skipped on its own. A computed property or a @ViewBuilder function inside the same view does not: it is just part of the parent’s body, and it re-runs whenever the parent does.

struct Dashboard: View {
    @State private var model = DashboardModel()

    var body: some View {
        VStack {
            header           // re-runs whenever Dashboard's body runs
            ChartView(points: model.points) // can be skipped if `points` didn't change
        }
    }

    private var header: some View {
        Text(model.title).font(.largeTitle)
    }
}

Computed properties are fine for organizing code. Extract a real subview when a part of the screen is expensive, or depends on only a small slice of the data.

@Observable tracks what you read

How precisely views are invalidated depends on how you model your data:

  • With ObservableObject, any @Published property change fires objectWillChange, and every view observing that object is invalidated, even views that never read the changed property.
  • With the @Observable macro (iOS 17+), SwiftUI records which properties each body actually read and invalidates a view only when one of those properties changes.

Either way, the dependency is on what body reads. A view that receives a whole model but displays a single property still depends on that model; with ObservableObject that means more invalidations than necessary.

Identity decides whether state survives

To match “old” and “new” views, SwiftUI uses identity:

  • Structural identity comes from a view’s type and its position in the hierarchy. The branches of an if/else in a @ViewBuilder are different positions (under the hood the result is a _ConditionalContent with two slots), so they count as different views.
  • Explicit identity comes from ForEach (via Identifiable or id:) and from the .id(_:) modifier.

When identity changes, SwiftUI treats the old view as removed and the new one as inserted. Its state is destroyed and recreated, and transitions play instead of in-place animations.

AnyView deserves a mention here. It erases the wrapped view’s type, so SwiftUI can no longer see the structure statically. When the type inside an AnyView changes, SwiftUI has to throw away the old content and build the new one. AnyView works, but prefer @ViewBuilder, Group, or some View when you can.

Animations interpolate data, not views

SwiftUI doesn’t animate by “comparing old and new views”. When a change happens inside a transaction that carries an animation (for example via withAnimation), SwiftUI interpolates animatable data, such as positions, sizes, opacities, or a shape’s animatableData, from the old value to the new one over time. Views that are inserted or removed use transitions. Identity matters here too: the same view with a new value animates in place, while a view with new identity gets a transition.

Bugs That Come From Forgetting Views Are Values

1. Expecting @State to follow a new value passed in

struct Editor: View {
    @State private var text: String

    init(initialText: String) {
        _text = State(initialValue: initialText)
    }

    var body: some View {
        TextField("Text", text: $text)
    }
}

State(initialValue:) is used only when the view’s identity is first created. When the parent later passes a different initialText, a new Editor struct is made, but SwiftUI keeps the existing storage and ignores the new initial value. If the parent owns the data, take a @Binding instead. If you really want to reset the state, give the view a new identity with .id(someKey).

2. Creating a model with @ObservedObject

struct ProfileView: View {
    @ObservedObject var model = ProfileModel() // ❌
    // ...
}

@ObservedObject does not own its object. Every time the parent re-evaluates its body, a new ProfileView struct is created, and with it a brand-new ProfileModel. Anything the old model had loaded is lost. If the view creates and owns the object, use @StateObject (or @State with an @Observable class on iOS 17+). Use @ObservedObject only for objects that someone else owns and passes in.

A related subtlety: with @StateObject and @State, the default-value expression still runs every time the struct is initialized. SwiftUI just discards the extra instances and keeps the original. Keep model initializers cheap, or create the model lazily (for example in .task).

3. Doing work in init or body

Because view values are created and discarded freely, an init that starts a network request, or a body that sorts a large array or formats dates with a fresh DateFormatter, will repeat that work more often than you expect. Put side effects in .task, .onAppear, or .onChange(of:), which are tied to the view’s identity, and move expensive work into your model.

4. A .task that keeps using an old value

Closures inside a view capture a copy of the view struct at the moment they’re created. Plain properties in that copy never change:

struct ArticleView: View {
    let articleID: Article.ID
    @State private var article: Article?

    var body: some View {
        content
            .task {
                article = try? await api.fetch(articleID) // ❌ runs once
            }
    }
}

.task starts when the view appears and is tied to the view’s identity, not to its inputs. If the parent keeps the same ArticleView on screen but passes a new articleID, the task doesn’t run again, and the screen keeps showing the old article. Tell SwiftUI what the task depends on:

.task(id: articleID) {
    article = try? await api.fetch(articleID) // ✅ cancelled and restarted when articleID changes
}

The same reasoning applies to .onAppear, and to any long-running work (timers, async sequences) that captured self when it started.

5. Unstable identities in ForEach

ForEach(items.indices, id: \.self) { index in
    ItemRow(item: items[index])
}

Here the identity of each row is its position. Delete the first item and every row below it gets a new item but keeps its old identity, which means it also keeps the old row’s @State. Text fields show the wrong text, toggles stay in the wrong state, and animations slide the wrong rows. The same thing happens with id: \.self on values that can repeat or change.

Use a stable, unique identifier that belongs to the data:

ForEach(items) { item in // Item: Identifiable, with a stable id
    ItemRow(item: item)
}

And avoid generating ids on the fly, such as let id = UUID() in a struct you re-create from the server on every refresh. A new id is a new identity, and the row resets.

6. Accidentally resetting state with identity changes

if isCompact {
    DetailView(item: item)
} else {
    DetailView(item: item)
        .padding()
}

These are two different DetailViews as far as SwiftUI is concerned, because they sit in different branches. Toggling isCompact destroys one and creates the other, which resets any @State inside. Prefer a single view whose modifiers depend on the condition:

DetailView(item: item)
    .padding(isCompact ? 0 : 16)

The same applies to .id(UUID()): it generates a new identity on every body evaluation and resets the view each time. The popular .if(condition) { $0.padding() } helper extension has the same problem, because it is just an if/else in disguise.

Seeing It for Yourself

You don’t have to take any of this on faith. SwiftUI has a debugging helper that prints why a view’s body ran:

var body: some View {
    let _ = Self._printChanges()
    // ...
}

Each time body runs, it prints the view name and what changed, for example ArticleView: @self, _article changed. Here @self means the view value itself was different from the previous one, and _article is the @State storage. On iOS 17 and later, Self._logChanges() does the same thing through the unified logging system. Both start with an underscore because they are meant for debugging only, so don’t ship them.

For real performance work, use the SwiftUI template in Instruments, which shows how often each view’s body runs and how long it takes.

Comparison with UIKit

In UIKit you write two code paths: one that builds the UI, and one that updates it when data changes (setting label.text, calling tableView.reloadData(), and so on). Forgetting an update in the second path is a classic source of UI that’s out of sync with the data.

SwiftUI merges these into one path: body describes the UI for the current state, and SwiftUI works out what to change. You still handle events (button actions, gestures, onChange), but those handlers update state, not views. The UI follows from the state.

The trade-off is control. In UIKit you decide exactly when each object is created, updated, and destroyed. In SwiftUI you give that up, and in exchange you have to describe identity and dependencies correctly so SwiftUI can make those decisions for you.

Conclusion

A SwiftUI view is a cheap, disposable description of UI, not the UI itself. SwiftUI keeps the real, long-lived structure, along with your state, in its own graph and matches new descriptions to it by identity.

Once you keep the two lifetimes apart (short-lived view values versus long-lived view identity), most of SwiftUI’s surprises make sense:

  • Put state that must persist in @State, @StateObject, or an @Observable model, never in plain stored properties.
  • Use @Binding or @ObservedObject for data owned by someone else.
  • Keep init and body cheap and free of side effects.
  • Use .task(id:) and .onChange(of:) when work depends on an input that can change.
  • Give ForEach stable, unique ids, and be deliberate about identity everywhere else, because changing it resets state.
  • When in doubt, add Self._printChanges() and watch what actually happens.

Further Reading

  • Demystify SwiftUI (WWDC21): identity, lifetime, and dependencies.
  • Discover Observation in SwiftUI (WWDC23): how @Observable tracks dependencies.
  • Demystify SwiftUI performance (WWDC23): dependencies, identity, and what makes updates slow.
entry.summary: In SwiftUI, a view is not a long-lived object sitting on screen. It is a lightweight value, usually a struct, that describes a piece of UI. SwiftUI creates these values, reads them, and throws them away constantly.

entry.title: This Is Why I Don’t Prefer Git GUI Tools

link.title: This Is Why I Don’t Prefer Git GUI Tools

entry.content:
Almost anyone who uses Xcode can quickly notice that it lacks many essential Git features, which is acceptable in some way since it’s primarily a development environment rather than a dedicated source control application.

The features available in Xcode may suffice for personal or small projects, but when working within a larger team, relying solely on the IDE can lead to significant challenges in managing source control effectively.

Managing Git history directly from the command line

Xcode's Source Control

Many engineers have also observed that file status markers like “A” (added), “M” (modified), and “C” (conflicted) often remain stuck, making it difficult to determine the current state of files at a glance.

Convincing backend engineers to use the terminal is relatively straightforward, as GUI tools do not automatically update the repository’s trunk on a server daily at 1:30 AM. However, a cron job that utilizes the CLI can easily perform this task. On the other hand, persuading mobile developers may be more challenging since the need for terminal usage is not always immediately apparent.

Real-Life Examples of Using the Git CLI

Let’s explore a few real-life examples that highlight the advantages of using the Git CLI over GUI tools. While I could list numerous cases, I will keep this post concise by focusing on a couple of key commands that illustrate the power of the terminal.

1. PR Reverts

GitHub introduced a feature for reverting pull requests (PRs). If you have an already merged PR and need to revert it before a tight deadline, using GitHub’s built-in revert feature does not provide details about which commits will be removed. This can lead to accidentally removing unrelated commits.

By contrast, using the command:

git revert --no-commit someHash

gives you fine-grained control over which commits to remove or retain, allowing for a more precise and safe rollback.

2. Submodules

When dealing with nested Git repositories (submodules), many GUI tools lack robust support for managing these structures. The Git CLI, however, provides comprehensive commands to add, update, and manage submodules effectively.

I typically keep the terminal open throughout the day; I can’t imagine working without it. I prefer understanding exactly what each command does rather than relying on button clicks in a GUI. While tools may come and go, the CLI remains the foundation upon which GUI tools are built.

The Benefits of Using the Git CLI

Using the command line allows for the convenient setup of install scripts, build scripts, deployment scripts, and more. In a large team setting, it is often unclear what exactly happens within a GUI-based application. I’ve witnessed colleagues make irreversible mistakes that could only be rectified using the CLI.

I find that I am several times more productive using the command line compared to navigating through menus with a mouse. While Git GUI tools aim to simplify the process, they can inadvertently add complexity, especially in larger projects. I’ve encountered non-standard terminology in some GUI tools that can make understanding Git more difficult.

Xcode comes with a diffing tool, which visualize differences effectively. However, for serious Git users, mastering the command line is crucial. It provides the flexibility, control, and efficiency needed to manage complex projects and collaborate effectively with team members.

Common Git Commands

Here is a table of common Git commands that I frequently use, sorted alphabetically, along with their descriptions:

Command Description
git add Stages changes in your working directory for the next commit.
git annotate Displays the last modification of each line in a file, showing who made the change and when.
git bisect Uses binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug.
git blame Shows what revision and author last modified each line of a file.
git checkout Switches branches or restores working tree files.
git checkout -b Creates a new branch and switches to it.
git cherry-pick Applies the changes introduced by an existing commit to your current branch.
git clean -fdx Removes untracked files from your working directory, including ignored files.
git clone Creates a copy of a remote repository on your local machine.
git clone --single-branch Clones only the specified branch from a remote repository.
git commit Records changes to the repository with a descriptive message.
git commit --amend -m "New commit message." Modifies the most recent commit with a new commit message.
git config Configures Git settings, such as user information and repository-specific options.
git diff Shows changes between commits, commit and working tree, etc.
git diff --check Checks for whitespace errors in the changes.
git fetch Downloads objects and refs from another repository without merging.
git gc Cleans up unnecessary files and optimizes the local repository.
git init Initializes a new Git repository in the current directory.
git log Displays the commit history for the current branch.
git log --all Shows the commit history for all branches.
git log --oneline Displays a simplified view of the commit history, showing one line per commit.
git log --summary Provides a summary of changes made in each commit, including file additions and deletions.
git log -p Shows the patch (diff) introduced in each commit.
git merge Combines changes from different branches into the current branch.
git pull --rebase Fetches changes from a remote repository and rebases your current branch on top of them.
git push Uploads local repository content to a remote repository.
git push --set-upstream origin Sets the default remote branch for the current local branch.
git push -u origin feature_branch_name Pushes the local branch to the remote repository and sets it to track the remote branch.
git rebase Reapplies commits on top of another base tip, allowing for a cleaner project history.
git remote -av Displays the remote repositories associated with the local repository.
git remote add Adds a new remote repository to your local Git configuration.
git reset --hard Resets the current branch to the specified state, discarding all changes in the working directory.
git restore Restores files in the working directory to their last committed state.
git revert Creates a new commit that undoes the changes made by a previous commit.
git rm Removes files from the working directory and stages the removal for the next commit.
git shortlog Summarizes the commit history, grouped by author.
git show Displays information about a specific commit, including changes and commit message.
git stash Temporarily saves changes in your working directory that are not ready to be committed.
git stash list Lists all stashed changes.
git stash pop Restores the most recently stashed changes and removes them from the stash list.
git status Displays the state of the working directory and the staging area, showing which files are staged, modified, or untracked.
git tag Creates a tag reference for a specific commit, often used for marking release points.
git worktree Manages multiple working trees attached to the same repository, allowing you to work on different branches simultaneously.
entry.summary: Almost anyone who uses Xcode can quickly notice that it lacks many essential Git features, which is acceptable in some way since it’s primarily a development environment rather than a dedicated source control application.

entry.title: Why I Prefer To Store My Files On A Digital Ocean Space & Not Google Drive Or Dropbox.

link.title: Why I Prefer To Store My Files On A Digital Ocean Space & Not Google Drive Or Dropbox.

entry.content:
This is not directly related to swift or iOS, but thought it’s worth sharing, since I couldn’t find any article that mention such way to backup files.

I’m one of those who experienced the evolution of data storage firsthand, starting with floppy disks to back up HTML pages—specifically 3DMax tutorials—during my visits to internet cafés back in 2003. As technology advanced, I transitioned to using CDs, followed by DVDs, which offered greater storage capacity.

Backing up files to object storage

I vividly remember the first flash drive my father gifted me as a teenager; it had a mere 128 MB of storage. At that time, such a device was considered a luxury and not affordable for many where I live. Fast forward to today, and we now have SSDs that are over 1000 times larger in capacity and available at significantly lower prices.

Cloud Storage

In the realm of cloud storage, common solutions like Google Drive and Dropbox offer plans, such as a 2TB option for $10 monthly. However, I prefer utilizing my own mountable drive integrated with a Content Delivery Network (CDN) for distributing my files efficiently. The best solution I’ve found for storing my work is using DigitalOcean Spaces, which is similar to AWS S3. I can conveniently mount it using a client like Cyberduck on my Mac, or on any device I own, allowing for seamless access and management of my files. This approach not only provides me with greater control over my data but also enhances my ability to share and distribute content effectively.

Cyberduck, showing a Digital Ocean drive

Serving static websites on DigitalOcean Spaces is entirely feasible by leveraging its S3-compatible object storage capabilities. To get started, you can upload your HTML, CSS, and JavaScript files directly to a Space, which acts as a repository for your website assets.

Even serving static websites, such as React applications or Jekyll blogs, on DigitalOcean Spaces is entirely feasible by leveraging its S3-compatible object storage capabilities. To get started, you can upload your website files—whether they are HTML, CSS, JavaScript. For example, when deploying a React app, you can build your project and upload the contents of the build folder to the Space. Similarly, for a Jekyll blog, you can generate the static site and upload the resulting files to your Space. Although DigitalOcean Spaces doesn’t natively support custom domains, you can set up a reverse proxy server using NGINX on a DigitalOcean Droplet to map your domain to the Space, allowing your static site to be accessed via your custom URL. This combination of tools enables you to efficiently serve your static websites while taking advantage of the scalability and performance of DigitalOcean’s infrastructure.

Pros & Cons

When considering a storage solution, it’s essential to weigh the advantages and disadvantages to determine the best fit for your needs. DigitalOcean Spaces offers a range of benefits that make it an appealing choice for developers and businesses alike. From cost-effectiveness to enhanced control over your files, the pros of using DigitalOcean Spaces can significantly enhance your workflow and file management capabilities. Below, we outline the key advantages of utilizing DigitalOcean Spaces, as well as some potential drawbacks to keep in mind, ensuring you have a comprehensive understanding of this powerful storage solution.

Pros

  • Direct Links: Easily access your files with straightforward URLs, allowing for seamless integration into your applications and workflows.

  • Cost-Effective: With plans starting as low as $5, DigitalOcean Spaces provides an economical solution for storing and serving your data, making it accessible for individuals and small businesses alike.

  • Bandwidth Savings: Setting up a Content Delivery Network (CDN) is simple, enabling you to save significant amounts of bandwidth and avoid exceeding transfer caps, which is especially beneficial for high-traffic applications.

  • Granular Control: You have total control over metadata and content types of your files. For example, you can specify whether an uploaded MP4 file is streamable or downloadable, tailoring the user experience to your needs.

  • Cross-Device Compatibility: DigitalOcean Spaces can be easily mounted on any device or server, providing flexibility and accessibility regardless of your operating system or hardware.

  • Active File Serving: Unlike traditional storage solutions, your files are actively served, allowing you to host dynamic content, such as an Angular website, without placing additional load on your server.

  • Custom URL Masking: You can mask the URL to reflect your own domain, enhancing professionalism and branding when presenting to clients or stakeholders during demos.

Cons

  • Technical Knowledge Requirement: Some users may find that utilizing DigitalOcean Spaces requires a certain level of technical knowledge, which could be a barrier for those unfamiliar with cloud storage solutions.

  • Limited Client Options: Many desktop clients used to mount such drives are not open source or free, which may limit accessibility for some users.

  • File Sharing Limitations: Files stored in DigitalOcean Spaces cannot be shared with specific individuals; they are either public or private, which may not suit all collaboration needs.

Security

DigitalOcean Spaces offers robust security features designed to protect your data effectively. One of the key aspects is access control, which allows users to manage permissions for files stored in Spaces.

Use cases are infinite!

The versatility of DigitalOcean Spaces opens up a myriad of use cases that can significantly enhance productivity and efficiency. For instance, if you’re involved in web scraping, you can effortlessly download large YouTube channels as a background job on the server. This approach allows you to avoid consuming your internet bandwidth while eliminating the need to keep a device running for extended periods. Instead, the files are stored directly in your DigitalOcean Space, making them readily accessible whenever you need them, without the hassle of local storage management. 🧐

Moreover, DigitalOcean Spaces functions similarly to a Network Attached Storage (NAS) solution, providing a centralized location for all your files that can be accessed from multiple devices. This capability is particularly beneficial for teams or individuals who require seamless file sharing and collaboration. Additionally, it can serve as a media center, allowing you to host and stream your multimedia content efficiently. Whether you’re managing a portfolio of projects, sharing resources with colleagues, or simply organizing personal media, the possibilities are truly endless with DigitalOcean Spaces.

Another innovative use case for DigitalOcean Spaces is as a centralized repository for continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines. Software engineers can utilize Spaces to store build artifacts, such as compiled binaries, Docker images, or deployment packages, generated during the CI/CD process. By configuring your CI/CD tools to upload these artifacts directly to DigitalOcean Spaces, you can ensure that all necessary files are easily accessible for deployment across various environments. This setup not only streamlines the deployment process but also provides a reliable and scalable solution for managing versioned artifacts, making it easier to roll back to previous versions if needed. Additionally, you can integrate Spaces with other services, such as monitoring and alerting tools, to keep track of deployment statuses and ensure smooth operations throughout the software development lifecycle.

I’d love to hear how others are using DigitalOcean Spaces in their projects! Whether you’re leveraging it for web hosting, data storage, or as part of your CI/CD pipeline, your experiences and tips could be incredibly valuable. Share your thoughts and use cases in the comments below—let’s learn from each other!
